mainTopic: The sources for שן and רגל in the פסוק, and the search for רב פפא's תולדות that are not like their אב.
overview: The amud begins by checking the ברייתא's proofs that "וְשִׁלַּח" means רגל and "וּבִעֵר" means שן. Each proof turns out to be needed: without it, we might have read both words as two cases of the same damage. Once each word has its own category, the גמרא compares them, so each teaches the other a detail. שן counts even when the item is not fully destroyed, and רגל counts even when the animal went by itself. The גמרא then asks why the תורה did not write only "וְשִׁלַּח", since the root שלח is used for both feet and teeth. The final answer is that "וּבִעֵר" teaches liability even when the animal was not sent. Next the גמרא looks for רב פפא's תולדות that are not like their אב. The תולדות of שן and of רגל turn out to share their אב's features. So the search moves to בור: first a nine-טפחים pit, which is rejected, then a stone, knife or load left in רשות הרבים. The amud ends as the גמרא starts asking exactly what case that is, and the discussion continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Finishing the verse that proves 'ובער' means eating
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא completes its proof-verse from מלכים א, which shows that the word "ובער" refers to שן.
steps.simpleTranslation: "...the dung, until it is all gone."
steps.whatsHappening: This is just the end of a פסוק the ברייתא was quoting on the previous lines. It wraps up the proof that "וּבִעֵר" means שן, damage by eating.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The verb ביעור in this פסוק describes something being totally consumed until nothing is left. That is how an animal's eating destroys what it eats, so the ברייתא reads "וּבִעֵר" as שן. This idea of total destruction comes back in step 5.

keyTerms.meaning: dung
until it is completely finished
"and it consumed": the word the ברייתא reads as שן (eating)

phrases.english: the dung, until it is all gone."
phrases.notes: This finishes מלכים א 14:10, which the ברייתא quoted to show that ביעור means eating something up completely.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the proof-verse begun before this section.
steps.raayaSupportSource: מלכים א 14:10, "כאשר יבער הגלל עד תמו".

steps.title: 'And he sends forth' means trampling with the foot
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the ברייתא: "וְשִׁלַּח" refers to רגל, proven from ישעיהו's phrase "משלחי רגל השור והחמור".
steps.simpleTranslation: The Master said: "And he sends forth" means the foot. So it says: "that send forth the feet of the ox and the donkey."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings up another line of the ברייתא it just quoted, so it can look into it. The line says that "וְשִׁלַּח" means רגל, and it brings a פסוק as proof.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא links the word "שִׁלַּח" to a פסוק where the same root appears right next to the word "רגל". That shared language is its proof. The next step will ask whether this proof was even necessary.

keyTerms.meaning: "and he sends forth" (שמות 22:4)
foot: the category of damage done by an animal trampling as it walks
"and so it says": introduces a supporting פסוק

phrases.english: The Master said:
"And he sends forth" — this is the foot,
and so it says:
"that send forth the feet of the ox and the donkey."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the ברייתא's proof for שן to its proof for רגל.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: "וְשִׁלַּח" in the פסוק refers to רגל, as shown by "משלחי רגל השור והחמור".

steps.title: Why is a proof needed? Goring and eating are already written
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the ברייתא: even without the ישעיהו proof, "וְשִׁלַּח" could only mean רגל, because קרן and שן each have their own פסוק.
steps.simpleTranslation: The ברייתא relies on the פסוק "that send forth the feet." But without it, how else could you explain "וְשִׁלַּח"? As goring? Goring is already written. As eating? Eating is already written.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why the ברייתא needed a proof at all. It argues that there is no other way to read "וְשִׁלַּח" anyway.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each type of damage has its own place in the תורה. קרן is written separately, and שן is taught by "וּבִעֵר". So the only category left for "וְשִׁלַּח" is רגל, which makes the ישעיהו proof look unnecessary.

keyTerms.meaning: the reason: "the only reason is...", used to draw an inference
"the Merciful One": a name for ה׳ as author of the תורה
but if not for this
how would you explain it?
horn: the category of goring
it is written (in its own פסוק)

phrases.english: The reason is that the Merciful One wrote
"that send forth the feet of the ox and the donkey";
but if not for this,
how would you have explained it?
If as goring — that is already written!
If as eating — that is already written!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges whether the proof in step 2 was necessary.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's use of ישעיהו 32:20 to prove that "ושלח" is רגל.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: קרן and שן are each written elsewhere, so the process of elimination already leaves only רגל, and the proof adds nothing.

steps.title: The proof was needed: we might have read both words as eating
steps.stepSummary: Without the ישעיהו proof, we might have thought "וּבִעֵר" and "וְשִׁלַּח" both describe שן. One would cover a case where the item is completely destroyed, and the other a case where it is not. The proof teaches that "וְשִׁלַּח" is רגל.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was needed. You might have thought both words are about eating: one where the damaged item is totally destroyed, and one where it is not. So the פסוק teaches us otherwise.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. It shows a real mistake we could have made without the ישעיהו proof.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Two different words for שן could each be covering a separate case. "וּבִעֵר" ("until it is all gone") would cover full destruction, and "וְשִׁלַּח" would cover partial damage. If so, nothing would be left over for רגל. The ישעיהו פסוק rules this out and assigns "וְשִׁלַּח" to רגל.

keyTerms.meaning: it was needed
you might have thought: introduces a mistaken assumption (הוה אמינא)
both this one and that one
the item itself is completely destroyed
it teaches us (that this is not so)

steps.whatToRemember: The ישעיהו פסוק is not extra. Without it, we could have split "וּבִעֵר" and "וְשִׁלַּח" between two kinds of שן damage: full destruction and partial damage. That would leave no source for רגל.
steps.confusionAlert: Here קַרְנָא does not mean "horn" (קֶרֶן, goring). It means the main item, the damaged object itself.

phrases.english: It was needed;
it could have entered your mind to say:
both this one and that one are about the tooth,
phrases.notes: "This one and that one" are the two words "וּבִעֵר" and "וְשִׁלַּח".

phrases.english: and that one is where the item is completely destroyed,
phrases.notes: Here קַרְנָא means the damaged object itself, not a horn. Literally, "the main thing."

phrases.english: this one is where the item is not completely destroyed;
so it teaches us otherwise.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 3.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Necessity (אצטריך): shows a mistaken reading the proof prevents.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Both "ובער" and "ושלח" refer to שן: one where the item is fully destroyed, one where it is only partly damaged.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ישעיהו פסוק shows that "ושלח" refers to רגל.

steps.title: Where do we learn שן when the item is not fully destroyed?
steps.stepSummary: Now that וְשִׁלַּח means רגל, the גמרא asks for the source that שן is liable even when the damaged item is not fully destroyed.
steps.simpleTranslation: Now that we have said וְשִׁלַּח is about רגל, how do we know that an owner pays for שן when the item is not completely eaten up?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a follow-up question. In step 4 we used וְשִׁלַּח for רגל, so it is no longer free to teach the 'not fully destroyed' case of שן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word וּבִעֵר suggests total destruction, because it means burning or consuming until nothing is left. In step 4 we considered using וְשִׁלַּח for the partial-damage case of שן, but we gave that word to רגל. So the partial-damage case of שן now seems to have no source.

keyTerms.meaning: The item itself is completely destroyed
From where do we know it?
We have established or explained it as

phrases.english: And now that we have established it as referring to Foot damage,
phrases.notes: "It" is the word וְשִׁלַּח from step 4.

phrases.english: Tooth damage where the item itself is not completely destroyed —
from where do we know it?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Follows from the answer in step 4, which used up the word וְשִׁלַּח for רגל.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The source for liability in שן when the item is not fully destroyed.

steps.title: שן is compared to רגל
steps.stepSummary: שן is compared to רגל. Just as רגל makes no difference between full and partial destruction, the same is true for שן.
steps.simpleTranslation: We learn it by comparing to רגל. With רגל, it doesn't matter whether the item was fully destroyed or not. So too with שן, it doesn't matter.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question by comparing שן to רגל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רגל, learned from וְשִׁלַּח, covers every kind of damage, whether full or partial. Because שן and רגל are taught together, שן borrows that same full range. So the word וּבִעֵר does not limit שן to total destruction.

keyTerms.meaning: Similar to; compared to
It makes no difference

steps.whatToRemember: שן is liable whether or not the item is fully destroyed, just like רגל.

phrases.english: It is similar to Foot damage:

phrases.aramaic: מָה רֶגֶל – לָא שְׁנָא מִכַּלְיָא קַרְנָא,
phrases.english: just as with Foot, it makes no difference if the item is completely destroyed
or if the item is not completely destroyed;

phrases.aramaic: אַף שֵׁן – לָא שְׁנָא מִכַּלְיָא קַרְנָא,
phrases.english: so too with Tooth, it makes no difference if the item is completely destroyed
or if the item is not completely destroyed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 5.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: שן is compared to רגל, so it covers both full and partial destruction.

steps.title: Re-quoting the proof that 'and it consumed' means שן
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the ברייתא again: וּבִעֵר means שן, proven from the פסוק in מלכים א.
steps.simpleTranslation: The ברייתא said: "וּבִעֵר" means שן. And so it says, "as one consumes ... until it is all gone."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings back a line from the ברייתא so it can question it next. This is a setup for the next move.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is the same proof from step 1, quoted again on purpose. In steps 2–4 the גמרא asked why וְשִׁלַּח needed a proof. Now it will ask the same question about וּבִעֵר.

keyTerms.meaning: And so it says: introduces a supporting פסוק

phrases.english: The Master said:
"And it consumed": this is Tooth damage,
and so it says:
"As one consumes the dung until it is all gone."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to the ברייתא's first proof, from step 1, to examine it the same way וְשִׁלַּח was examined.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: וּבִעֵר refers to שן, proven from מלכים א 14:10.

steps.title: Why is a proof needed for 'and it consumed'?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the ברייתא needs the מלכים א proof, since קרן and רגל each already have their own words, so וּבִעֵר could only mean שן.
steps.simpleTranslation: So the only reason we read it as שן is the פסוק "as one consumes...". But without it, what else could it mean? קרן is already written elsewhere, and רגל is already written elsewhere!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the ברייתא, asking why it needs a proof-verse for וּבִעֵר at all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This copies the challenge from step 3. Each type of damage already has its own words in the תורה. So by simple elimination, וּבִעֵר would have to mean שן even without a proof.

keyTerms.meaning: The reason
The Merciful One, meaning ה׳ in the תורה
But if it were not so
It is written

phrases.english: The reason is that the Merciful One wrote
"as one consumes the dung until it is all gone,"
but if not for this,
how would we have explained it?
If as Horn damage, that is already written!
If as Foot damage, that is already written!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the proof just quoted in step 7.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's use of מלכים א to prove that וּבִעֵר means שן.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: By elimination, since קרן and רגל are already written, the proof-verse seems unnecessary.

steps.title: Without the proof, both words might have meant רגל
steps.stepSummary: The proof is needed. Otherwise we might have read both וּבִעֵר and וְשִׁלַּח as רגל: one for an animal wandering on its own, and one for an animal its owner sent.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is needed. You might have thought both words are about רגל: this one when the animal goes by itself, and that one when the owner sends it. The פסוק teaches us otherwise.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the מלכים א proof is needed to stop a wrong reading.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Without the proof, one could split רגל into two cases and give one word to each. The animal wandering on its own would be וּבִעֵר, and the animal sent by the owner would be וְשִׁלַּח. The מלכים א verse shows that וּבִעֵר means eating, so it is שן.

keyTerms.meaning: It is necessary
You might have thought to say
On its own
Actively sent it
It teaches us

steps.whatToRemember: Each proof-verse in the ברייתא is needed. Without the proofs, וּבִעֵר and וְשִׁלַּח could have been read as two cases of the same damage. The proofs show that וּבִעֵר is שן and וְשִׁלַּח is רגל.
steps.confusionAlert: This mirrors step 4 in reverse. There, both words might have been שן. Here, both words might have been רגל.

phrases.english: It is necessary;
it could have entered your mind to say:
both this and that refer to Foot damage,
this one where the animal goes on its own,
and that one where the owner actively sent it;
so it teaches us otherwise.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 8.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Shows the proof blocks a reasonable mistaken reading
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Both וּבִעֵר and וְשִׁלַּח mean רגל: one for an animal wandering on its own, and one for an animal sent by its owner.
steps.terutzMaskana: The verse in מלכים א shows that וּבִעֵר is שן.

steps.title: Where do we learn רגל when the animal went on its own?
steps.stepSummary: Since וּבִעֵר is now used for שן, and וְשִׁלַּח sounds like the owner sent the animal, the גמרא asks for the source that רגל is liable even when the animal went by itself.
steps.simpleTranslation: Now that we used the word וּבִעֵר for שן, where do we learn that an owner is liable for רגל when the animal went off and did damage by itself?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a new question. וְשִׁלַּח ("and he sends") sounds like the owner sent the animal, so where do we learn about an animal that walked off on its own?
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 9 the גמרא said we might have used both words for רגל: one for an animal that wandered on its own, and one for an animal its owner sent. Now that וּבִעֵר has been given to שן, only וְשִׁלַּח is left for רגל, and that word sounds like 'sent.' So the case of an animal that wandered on its own seems to have no source.

keyTerms.meaning: And now
That we applied it to (we set the word on this meaning)
By itself, on its own
From where do we know it?

phrases.english: And now that we have applied it to Eating (שן),
phrases.notes: "It" is the word וּבִעֵר, which step 7 proved means שן.

phrases.english: Trampling (רגל) where the animal went on its own: from where do we know it?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Follows from step 9: once וּבִעֵר is assigned to שן, the 'animal went on its own' case of רגל has lost its source.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The source for liability for רגל when the animal went by itself, without being sent.

steps.title: רגל is compared to שן
steps.stepSummary: Just as with שן it makes no difference whether the animal was sent or went by itself, the same is true for רגל.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is learned by comparing רגל to שן. With שן, it makes no difference if the owner sent the animal or it went by itself. So too with רגל, it makes no difference if the owner sent it or it went by itself.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers by comparing רגל to שן, the same kind of comparison it used in step 6, but now going the other way.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 6, שן learned from רגל that partial damage counts too. Now רגל learns from שן that 'went by itself' counts too. Each of the two words gives a detail to the other.

keyTerms.meaning: Similar to, compared to
It makes no difference
He actually sent it

steps.whyThisMatters: This shows the two words are read together. A detail found in one category carries over to the other.

phrases.english: It is similar to Eating (שן):

phrases.aramaic: מָה שֵׁן – לָא שְׁנָא שַׁלְּחַהּ שַׁלּוֹחֵי,
phrases.english: Just as with Eating, it makes no difference if he sent it,
or if it went on its own;

phrases.aramaic: אַף רֶגֶל – לָא שְׁנָא שַׁלְּחַהּ שַׁלּוֹחֵי,
phrases.english: so too with Trampling, it makes no difference if he sent it,
or if it went on its own.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 10.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רגל is compared to שן. Since שן is liable whether the animal was sent or went by itself, so is רגל.

steps.title: Why not write only וְשִׁלַּח, which means both?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges: the word וְשִׁלַּח can mean רגל and can also mean שן, so the תורה should have written only it and left out וּבִעֵר.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let the תורה write only "וְשִׁלַּח" and skip "וּבִעֵר." The word שלח is used for both רגל and שן. It is used for רגל, as it says "that send forth the feet of the ox and the donkey." It is used for שן, as it says "and the teeth of animals I will send against them."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the need for two words. It shows from two פסוקים that the word 'send' is used for feet and also for teeth.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If one word can cover both רגל and שן, then the second word, וּבִעֵר, looks extra. So why did the תורה write it?

keyTerms.meaning: The Merciful One, meaning the תורה
And there would be no need
It means, it can refer to

phrases.english: And let the Merciful One write "and he sends forth,"
and there would be no need for "and it consumed";
since it can mean Trampling and can mean Eating:
It means Trampling, as it is written:
"That send forth the feet of the ox and the donkey";
and it means Eating, as it is written:
"And the teeth of animals I will send forth against them"!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְלִכְתּוֹב רַחֲמָנָא וְשִׁלַּח וְלָא בָּעֵי וּבִעֵר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Now that the two words have been tied together, the גמרא asks why both are needed at all.
steps.kashyaTarget: The need for the word וּבִעֵר in the פסוק.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The root שלח is used in other פסוקים for both feet (רגל) and teeth (שן), so וְשִׁלַּח alone could cover both categories.

steps.title: With one word we would think it meant only one of them
steps.stepSummary: Without the extra word, we would read וְשִׁלַּח as meaning only one category, either רגל or שן, since each has a reason to be the main one.
steps.simpleTranslation: If not for the extra word in the פסוק, I would have said it means either this or that: either רגל, because its damage is common, or שן, because the animal gets pleasure from the damage.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that one word would not be enough. We would think it meant just one category, and each one has a good reason to be the one meant.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רגל could be the one meant because its damage happens often. שן could be the one meant because the animal enjoys the damage. Since we could not tell which, the תורה wrote a second word so that both are clearly included.

keyTerms.meaning: An extra word or phrase in the פסוק
I would have thought
Its damage is common
There is pleasure in its damage

steps.whatToRemember: וְשִׁלַּח means רגל and וּבִעֵר means שן, and each one teaches a detail to the other. This step's reason for needing both words does not hold up, though: step 14 rejects it, and step 15 gives the real reason.
steps.confusionAlert: The גמרא is not saying וְשִׁלַּח can't mean both. It is saying that with only one word, we would assume it meant just one of them, and we would not know which.

phrases.english: If not for the extra word in the verse,

phrases.aramaic: הֲוָה אָמֵינָא: אוֹ הָא אוֹ הָא –
phrases.english: I would have said: either this one or that one:
either Trampling, since its damage is common,
or Eating, since there is pleasure in its damage.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי לָאו קְרָא יַתִּירָה הֲוָה אָמֵינָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 12.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Shows that the second word is needed to stop us from limiting the פסוק to only one category.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: With only וְשִׁלַּח, the פסוק would mean just one category, either רגל (common damage) or שן (pleasure in the damage).
steps.terutzMaskana: The extra word וּבִעֵר makes sure both רגל and שן are included.

steps.title: If both readings are equal, include both
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא pushes back on Step 13. If רגל and שן have equally good claims on וְשִׁלַּח, the word should cover both of them, and וּבִעֵר would still be extra.
steps.simpleTranslation: Since the two readings are equal, let both be included. Which one could you leave out?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the answer it just gave. It says that if neither reading of וְשִׁלַּח is stronger, we would simply include both.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 13 said that without וּבִעֵר we would pick only one meaning for וְשִׁלַּח. The גמרא replies that when two options are exactly equal, you have no basis to choose one over the other, so the word covers both. That would make וּבִעֵר unnecessary again.

keyTerms.meaning: Since / after all (opens a line of reasoning)
Equal, balanced
Which of them would you exclude?

phrases.english: Since they are equal,
phrases.notes: He means רגל and שן, which each had a good reason to be the meaning of וְשִׁלַּח.

phrases.english: let both of them come (be included)
which of them would you leave out?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the answer of Step 13
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim in Step 13 that without וּבִעֵר we would read וְשִׁלַּח as only one category
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: When two readings are equally strong, neither one wins, so both are included. That makes וּבִעֵר extra.

steps.title: The extra word teaches liability even when the animal went on its own
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that וּבִעֵר is still needed. וְשִׁלַּח alone might cover both categories, but only when the owner sent the animal. וּבִעֵר teaches that the owner is liable even when the animal went by itself.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is needed. You might have thought this only applies when the owner sent the animal, but not when it went on its own. So the תורה teaches us otherwise.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא accepts that וְשִׁלַּח could cover both רגל and שן. It explains that וּבִעֵר still adds something new.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word וְשִׁלַּח means 'sent', so on its own it sounds like the owner sent the animal out. Without וּבִעֵר, we might have limited liability to cases where the owner sent the animal. וּבִעֵר teaches that the owner pays even when the animal wandered off by itself.

keyTerms.meaning: It is needed
You might have thought to say
On its own, by itself
It teaches us (that the mistaken idea is wrong)

steps.whatToRemember: וּבִעֵר and וְשִׁלַּח together teach that the owner pays for שן and רגל whether he sent the animal or it went out on its own.

phrases.english: It is needed;
it would have entered your mind to say:
this applies only where he actually sent it out,
but where it went on its own, not;
so the extra word teaches us otherwise.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 14
steps.terutzResolutionType: The extra word adds a new detail: liability even without the owner sending the animal
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Liability for רגל and שן would apply only when the owner sent the animal
steps.terutzMaskana: The owner is liable even when the animal went out by itself

steps.title: What is a sub-category of שן?
steps.stepSummary: Now that the sources are settled, the גמרא asks what counts as a תולדה of שן.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is a sub-category of שן?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new topic and asks for an example of a תולדה of שן. This sets up the next move, where it checks whether רב פפא's statement applies here.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier, רב פפא said that some אבות have תולדות that are not like them. To find out which אבות he meant, the גמרא first has to define the תולדות of each one, starting with שן.

keyTerms.meaning: A sub-category (literally 'offspring') of a main category of damage
Literally 'tooth': damage an animal does by eating

phrases.english: What is a sub-category of שן?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new section after the source derivations are finished
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A definition or example of a תולדה of שן

steps.title: Rubbing or messing things for its own pleasure
steps.stepSummary: A תולדה of שן is when an animal damages something for its own enjoyment without eating it, such as rubbing against a wall or dirtying produce.
steps.simpleTranslation: It rubbed against a wall for its pleasure, or it dirtied produce for its pleasure.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives two examples of a תולדה of שן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: What these cases share with שן is that the animal enjoys itself while doing the damage. The difference is that it is not eating.

keyTerms.meaning: It rubbed itself (to scratch an itch)
For its own pleasure
It dirtied or soiled

phrases.english: It rubbed against a wall for its pleasure,
or it dirtied produce for its pleasure.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 16
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Damage done for the animal's own pleasure without eating: rubbing on a wall or dirtying produce

steps.title: The sub-categories of שן share all its features
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what makes שן special and finds that its תולדות have the very same features. So they cannot be different from שן.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is special about שן? The animal gets pleasure from the damage, and it is your property, so guarding it is your job. These cases also have pleasure from the damage, are your property, and guarding them is your job!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tests whether the תולדות of שן could be the 'different' kind רב פפא spoke about. It finds no difference at all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The features that define שן are pleasure in the damage, the animal being your property, and your duty to guard it. All of these also appear in rubbing and dirtying. Since nothing is missing, there is no reason for these תולדות to have a different law.

keyTerms.meaning: What is different about...?
The animal gets pleasure from its damage
Guarding it is your responsibility

phrases.english: What is special about שן?
That there is pleasure in its damage,
and it is your property, and guarding it is on you;
these too have pleasure in their damage,
and they are your property, and guarding them is on you!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tests the examples of Step 17 against רב פפא's statement
steps.kashyaTarget: The possibility that רב פפא's 'different תולדות' refers to the תולדות of שן
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Every feature that defines שן also appears in its תולדות, so there is no basis for treating them differently.

steps.title: The תולדות of שן are like שן; רב פפא meant רגל
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא concludes that a תולדה of שן has the same law as שן. רב פפא's statement must be about the תולדות of רגל.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, a sub-category of שן is like שן. When רב פפא spoke, he meant a sub-category of רגל.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא draws its conclusion and moves רב פפא's statement over to רגל. This sets up the next question: what are the תולדות of רגל?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since the תולדות of שן match it completely, they cannot be the exception רב פפא described. So the 'different' תולדות must be found among the תולדות of רגל.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather (introduces a corrected conclusion)
Literally 'foot': damage an animal does while walking

steps.whatToRemember: A תולדה of שן has exactly the same law as שן. רב פפא's 'different' תולדות are found under רגל.

phrases.english: Rather, a sub-category of שן is like שן,
and when רב פפא spoke,
he meant a sub-category of רגל.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the conclusion from Step 18
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The תולדות of שן share its law. רב פפא was referring to the תולדות of רגל.

steps.title: What is a sub-category of רגל?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא now asks what counts as a תולדה of רגל.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is a sub-category of רגל?
steps.whatsHappening: Now that רב פפא's statement points to רגל, the גמרא asks for the תולדות of רגל. This sets up the list that follows.
steps.deeperAnalysis: To see how the תולדות of רגל differ from רגל, the גמרא first has to say what they are.

keyTerms.meaning: What is it?

phrases.english: What is a sub-category of רגל?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Follows up on the conclusion that רב פפא meant רגל
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A definition or examples of the תולדות of רגל

steps.title: Damage by the body, hair, or gear while walking
steps.stepSummary: The תולדות of רגל are cases where the animal causes damage while walking, but with something other than its feet: its body, its hair, a rope on it, a bit in its mouth, or a bell on its neck.
steps.simpleTranslation: It caused damage with its body as it walked, or with its hair as it walked, or with a rope on it, or with a bit in its mouth, or with a bell on its neck.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא lists five examples of a תולדה of רגל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Like רגל, these are ordinary damages that happen just from the animal walking around. The difference is that the damage comes from its body or from gear it carries, not from its feet.

keyTerms.meaning: In the course of its walking
A rope or harness on the animal
A bit or bridle in the animal's mouth
A bell

phrases.english: It caused damage with its body as it walked,
with its hair as it walked,
with a rope that is on it,
with a bit that is in its mouth,
with a bell that is on its neck.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 20
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Damage while walking, done by the body, hair, rope, bit, or bell rather than by the feet

steps.title: The תולדות of רגל have the same features as רגל
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what makes רגל special and shows that its תולדות have the exact same features.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is special about רגל? Its damage is common, the animal is your property, and guarding it is your job. But these תולדות are the same: their damage is common, they are your property, and guarding them is your job!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the idea that the תולדות of רגל could have a different law from רגל itself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רגל has three features: its damage happens often, the animal belongs to you, and you must guard it. Damage done while walking by the body, hair, or a bell has all three features too. So there is no reason to treat these תולדות differently from רגל.

keyTerms.meaning: What is different? What makes it special?
Its damage is common, it happens often
Your property
Guarding it is your responsibility

phrases.english: What is different about Trampling?
That its damage is common,
and it is your property, and guarding it is upon you;
these too, their damage is common,
phrases.notes: "These" means the offshoots of רגל from the last step: body, hair, rope, bit, bell.

phrases.english: and they are your property, and guarding them is upon you!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the same pattern as Step 18, which challenged שן. Now it challenges the תולדות of רגל listed in Step 21.
steps.kashyaTarget: The idea that the תולדות of רגל could differ in law from רגל
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Every feature that makes רגל special is also found in its תולדות, so they cannot have a different law.

steps.title: תולדות of רגל are like רגל, so רב פפא meant בור
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא concludes that a תולדה of רגל has the same law as רגל, so רב פפא must have been talking about the תולדות of בור.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, a תולדה of רגל is like רגל. When רב פפא spoke, he meant a תולדה of בור.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא closes the רגל discussion and moves רב פפא's statement over to בור.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב פפא had said that some תולדות are not like their אב. שן and רגל have now been ruled out. So the גמרא tries בור as the category he meant.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather (drops the earlier idea)
Pit, one of the four main categories of damage

steps.whatToRemember: The תולדות of both שן and רגל have the same law as their אב. The search for רב פפא's 'different' תולדה now moves to בור.

phrases.english: Rather, an offshoot of Trampling is like Trampling,
and when Rav Pappa said it,
it was about an offshoot of Pit.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the conclusion from the challenge in Step 22, the same way Step 19 did for שן.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: A תולדה of רגל has the same law as רגל. רב פפא's statement is now applied to בור.

steps.title: What is a תולדה of בור?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what counts as a תולדה of בור.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is a תולדה of בור?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a defining question to set up the next move: it needs to know what a תולדה of בור is before it can test רב פפא's claim.
steps.deeperAnalysis: To show that a תולדה of בור is different from its אב, we first need to know what that תולדה is. This question opens a new line of discussion.

keyTerms.meaning: What is it?

phrases.english: An offshoot of Pit, what is it?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Follows from Step 23's move to בור. The question has the same form as Step 20's question about רגל.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A definition of a תולדה of בור

steps.title: A ten-versus-nine split is rejected because the תורה gives no numbers
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests a ten-טפחים pit is the אב and a nine-טפחים pit is the תולדה, then objects that the תורה mentions neither number.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you say the אב is a pit ten טפחים deep and the תולדה is nine, that does not work. Neither nine nor ten is written in the תורה!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא offers a possible answer and immediately knocks it down.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An אב is supposed to be what the תורה writes, and a תולדה is something similar that is not written. The תורה gives no depth at all for the pit. So there is no basis for calling ten the written אב and nine the unwritten תולדה.

keyTerms.meaning: If you say (introduces a suggestion that will be rejected)
Main category, the one written in the תורה
They are written

phrases.english: If you say the main category is ten,
and the offshoot is nine;
nine is not written,
and ten is not written either!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Suggests an answer to Step 24's question and challenges it in the same breath.
steps.kashyaTarget: The suggestion that a ten-טפחים pit is the אב and a nine-טפחים pit is the תולדה
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: An אב must be written in the תורה, but the תורה gives no depth, so neither depth can be the written one.

steps.title: The תורה speaks of a dead animal, and only ten טפחים kills
steps.stepSummary: The תורה mentions the animal dying, and the רבנן knew that only a ten-טפחים pit kills. So the pit in the תורה is ten deep.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is not a problem. The תורה says 'and the dead animal shall be his.' The רבנן knew that a ten-טפחים pit kills, while a nine-טפחים pit injures but does not kill.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends the ten-versus-nine idea by showing that the number ten is hinted at in the תורה after all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק about בור speaks of an animal that died in the pit. The רבנן had a known fact that only a pit ten טפחים deep can kill. So the pit the תורה describes is ten deep, making it the אב, and the nine-טפחים pit is the תולדה.

keyTerms.meaning: This is not difficult
The Merciful One, meaning the תורה
The רבנן know it as an established fact
Death

phrases.english: This is not difficult;
"And the dead animal shall be his," says the Merciful One,
and the Sages know for certain,
that ten causes death,
nine causes injury,
but does not cause death.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in Step 25 by tying the number ten to the פסוק.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Ties the number to the פסוק through a known fact about pits
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Since the תורה gives no depth, it seemed impossible to call a ten-טפחים pit the written אב and a nine-טפחים pit its תולדה.
steps.terutzMaskana: The תורה speaks of death, and only ten טפחים kills, so the written pit is ten deep.

steps.title: Then each pit is its own main category
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects that a ten-טפחים pit would be the אב for killing and a nine-טפחים pit would be the אב for injuring.
steps.simpleTranslation: In the end, this one is an אב for killing, and that one is an אב for injuring!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the answer from the last step. The nine-טפחים pit does not look like a תולדה after all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The nine-טפחים pit is not a smaller copy of the ten-טפחים pit. It covers a different kind of harm, injury rather than death. So it seems to be its own main category for injuries, not a תולדה.

keyTerms.meaning: In the end, ultimately
Injuries, damages

steps.confusionAlert: The גמרא is not saying a nine-טפחים pit is exempt. It is only asking whether it should be called an אב or a תולדה.

phrases.english: In the end,
this one is a main category for death,
and that one is a main category for injuries!

steps.triggerLanguage: סוֹף סוֹף זֶה אָב לְמִיתָה וְזֶה אָב לִנְזָקִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer given in Step 26.
steps.kashyaTarget: Calling the nine-טפחים pit a תולדה of the ten-טפחים pit
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Each pit covers a different kind of harm, so each one is a main category of its own, and neither is an offshoot of the other.

steps.title: רב פפא meant a stone, knife, or load left in the street
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא gives a new answer: the תולדות of בור that are different from their אב are a stone, knife, or load left in רשות הרבים that caused damage.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רב פפא was talking about his stone, his knife, or his load that he left in the public domain, and they caused damage.
steps.whatsHappening: The pit-depth idea did not work, so the גמרא gives a new example of a תולדה of בור that רב פפא could have meant.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ten-versus-nine טפחים idea failed because each depth would be its own אב. Now the גמרא points to objects that are not holes at all: a stone, knife, or load left in the street. They trip people like a pit does, but they are a different kind of thing.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather; this brings a new answer in place of the one that failed
His stone, his knife, and his load
The public domain, a street or place everyone uses
They caused damage

phrases.english: Rather, he was talking about his stone,
his knife, or his load
that he placed in the public domain
and they caused damage.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the rejected pit-depth explanation from step 27 with a new example of a different תולדה of בור.
steps.terutzResolutionType: New case identification: re-applying רב פפא's statement to a different set of examples
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We thought the different תולדה of בור was a nine-טפחים pit.
steps.terutzMaskana: The different תולדה of בור is a stone, knife, or load left in רשות הרבים that caused damage.

steps.title: If the objects were made ownerless, they are just like a pit
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what case we are talking about. If the owner made the objects הפקר, then both רב and שמואל agree they are the same as בור, so they are not a 'different' תולדה.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the case? If he made them ownerless, then both according to רב and according to שמואל, this is the same as בור.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts testing the new answer by asking exactly what case we mean. This is a setup: it checks the first option here and will check the other option next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב פפא needs a תולדה that is different from בור. But if the owner gave up ownership of the stone or knife, everyone agrees it works just like a pit, so it is not different at all. This first option fails, and the גמרא will look at the case where he did not make them הפקר.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the case? How exactly does it look?
He made them ownerless (הֶפְקֵר), giving up ownership
Whether according to רַב or according to שְׁמוּאֵל
This is the same as

steps.confusionAlert: This is not the end of the argument. The גמרא only knocked out the ownerless case. It still has to look at the case where the owner kept ownership.

phrases.english: What is the case?
If he made them ownerless,
both according to רב and according to שמואל,
this is the same as a pit.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tests the new answer from step 28 by defining the case and rejecting its first option.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim in step 28 that a stone, knife, or load is a תולדה of בור that is different from its אב.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the objects were made הפקר, both רב and שמואל treat them exactly like בור. So in that case they are not different from the אב, and they cannot be what רב פפא meant.
